segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a reed like a staff was given to me, with the words,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Get up and measure the sanctuary of God and the altar and those who worship in it.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But leave out the courtyard outside the sanctuary and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I will grant it to my two witnesses to prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if anyone wants to harm them, fire comes out of their mouths and consumes their enemies; and if anyone should want to harm them, this is how that person must be killed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These have the authority to shut the sky, so that no rain falls during the days of their prophesying, and they have authority over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they finish their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war on them and conquer them and kill them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And their corpses lie on the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations look at their corpses for three and a half days, and they do not allow their corpses to be placed in a tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who live on the earth rejoice over them and celebrate, and they will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who live on the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who were watching them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come up here!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went up into heaven in the cloud, and their enemies watched them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell, and seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest became terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second woe has passed. Look, the third woe is coming soon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the twenty-four elders who sit before God on their thrones fell on their faces and worshiped God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, the one who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The nations were angry, and your anger has come, and the time for the dead to be judged, and to give the reward to your slaves the prophets and to the holy ones and to those who fear your name, the small and the great, and to destroy those who destroy the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And God's sanctuary in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his sanctuary; and there were flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder and an earthquake and heavy hail.

notes.traditional: and the angel stood, saying (KJV); and I was told
notes.note: The Greek has only the participle 'saying', with no stated speaker. 'My two witnesses' in verse 3 suggests God or Christ is speaking, or an angel on their behalf; some later manuscripts supply 'the angel stood', which the KJV follows. The speech is taken here to end at verse 3, since verse 4 refers to the Lord in the third person, but the Greek does not mark where it closes.

Most translations have 'temple'. The Greek word used here is the one for the sanctuary building itself, the dwelling place of the deity, as distinct from the wider temple precinct with its courts. That distinction matters in this passage, where the outer courtyard lies outside what is measured. The same word is used for God's sanctuary in heaven in verse 19.

One Greek word means both 'nations' and, in Jewish usage, 'Gentiles' (the non-Jewish peoples). Older translations have 'Gentiles' here, and the trampling of the holy city by foreigners supports that nuance. 'Nations' is used because Revelation consistently has the peoples of the whole world in view; the same word appears in verses 9 and 18.

Forty-two months, the 1,260 days of verse 3, and three and a half years are the same span. It echoes the 'time, times and half a time' of Daniel (7:25; 12:7), a limited period in which God's people are oppressed. The three and a half days of verses 9 and 11 play on the same figure.

notes.phrase: the two olive trees and the two lampstands
notes.note: The image comes from Zechariah 4, where a lampstand is flanked by two olive trees identified as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. These are usually understood as the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua. In Revelation 1:20 lampstands stand for churches.

The powers described recall Elijah, who announced a drought and called down fire on his enemies (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 1), and Moses, who turned water to blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). Whether the two witnesses are meant to be particular individuals, such as Moses and Elijah returned, or a symbol of the witnessing church is disputed.

'Where their Lord also was crucified' points to Jerusalem, and many interpreters take it so. Elsewhere in Revelation, however, 'the great city' is Babylon, generally understood as Rome. Others therefore read it as a symbol of the world city hostile to God wherever it is found. The text does not settle the question.

Most modern translations have 'symbolically' or 'figuratively'. The word is literally 'spiritually', and elsewhere in the New Testament it means in a manner belonging to or given by the Spirit. The sense is probably that the names Sodom and Egypt express the city's true character as the Spirit discloses it, which is more than a figure of speech, so the older rendering is kept.

notes.traditional: the Spirit of life (KJV); a breath of life
notes.note: The Greek word means both 'breath' and 'spirit', so 'a spirit of life' or 'the Spirit of life' is also possible. The wording echoes Ezekiel 37, where breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, so 'breath' is chosen. A first-century reader would likely have heard both senses.

notes.phrase: the one who is and who was
notes.traditional: which art, and wast, and art to come (KJV)
notes.note: Some later manuscripts add 'and who is to come', matching the fuller formula in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8; the KJV follows them. The earliest and best witnesses lack the phrase here. The shorter form fits the context: God's coming is no longer future, because he has begun to reign.

Most translations have 'servants'. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone owned by a master, and that is how a first-century reader heard it. 'My slaves the prophets' is a standing phrase in the Greek Old Testament, where it is a title of honor for those wholly at God's disposal.

Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'. 'Saints' now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel.

notes.traditional: thy wrath is come; your wrath has come
notes.note: Most translations have 'the nations were angry' (or 'raged') and then 'your wrath'. The Greek uses a verb and a noun from the same root, setting the anger of the nations against the anger of God, so one English word is used for both. The verse closes with a similar play, 'destroy those who destroy'.

candidates.reason: Distinct from ἱερόν (the temple complex) and traditionally also rendered 'temple'; needs one decision across the Gospels, Paul ('you are God's ναός') and Revelation.
Translators split between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant', and the choice recurs in every part of the New Testament, including set phrases like 'slaves the prophets'.
'Wrath' versus 'anger' for God's ὀργή recurs in Paul, the Gospels and Revelation, and should not vary; the relation to θυμός also needs fixing.
A key word in Revelation and the Johannine letters, rendered variously as 'conquer', 'overcome' or 'be victorious'; readers need to see it is the same word for the beast and for believers.

candidates.rendering: forever and ever (in εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων)
candidates.reason: The 'ages of ages' formula and αἰών generally ('age', 'world', 'forever') recur throughout and need one policy on whether to keep the Semitic plural idiom.
